claims.statement: Mesopotamian kings treated dreams as portents and consulted specialist interpreters.
claims.reasoning: Wikipedia (Daniel 2) reports royal dreams as portents and a Nabonidus inscription recording a dream of Nebuchadnezzar; Oppenheim's standard study of the dream literature exists but was not read.
limitations: Secondary evidence only; primary dream texts not consulted this session.

claims.statement: Nebuchadnezzar had this dream and Daniel recounted and interpreted it.
claims.reasoning: No Babylonian or other independent source mentions the dream, the decree against the wise men, or Daniel. This is not a disproof.

claims.statement: The content of the dream was revealed to Daniel by God.
claims.reasoning: Divine revelation cannot be assessed by historical or scientific methods. This is not a theological verdict.

claims.statement: "The second year of Nebuchadnezzar" (Dan 2:1) is chronologically compatible with the three-year training of Daniel 1.
claims.reasoning: Chronology engine. Dan 2:1's "second year" falls Feb 603 BC – May 602 BC if Nebuchadnezzar's years are counted with an accession year (Babylonian practice), or Feb 604 BC – May 603 BC if his accession year is counted as year 1. Assumption (not textual): a campaign by Nebuchadnezzar against Jerusalem (Dan 1:1) could not precede Carchemish, the first Babylonian operation in the west recorded in ABC 5 (Mar 605 BC – Aug 605 BC). Three full years of training after that end no earlier than Mar 602 BC – Aug 602 BC, i.e. at the very end of or after the accession-reckoned "second year" and well after the non-accession one. Full-year counting therefore fits only at the extreme margin (if at all); counting partial years inclusively (accession year, year 1, year 2) fits comfortably. Guzik proposes the inclusive/overlap explanation; the critical view treats chapters 1 and 2 as originally independent tales.
limitations: Depends on the assumption that the Dan 1:1 campaign followed Carchemish.

evidence.finding: Royal dreams were regarded as portents; an inscription of Nabonidus records a dream in which Nebuchadnezzar appears to reassure him.
Guzik notes that overlapping regnal-year counts allow 602 BC to be both Nebuchadnezzar's second year and after the training.
The king's need to be introduced to Daniel after 1:18–20, the language switch and repetitions are cited as evidence that chapters 1 and 2 were not composed as one continuous narrative.
Josephus retells the dream and its interpretation (late 1st century AD), dependent on the biblical account.
A Roman-era fragment (Aemilius Sura) lists a succession of world empires — Assyria, Media, Persia, Macedonia, then Rome — showing that four-empire schemes circulated in the Hellenistic-Roman world.
limitations: Date of the fragment debated (early 2nd vs 1st century BC).

research_gaps: Primary Mesopotamian dream texts (Oppenheim 1956) not read.
Collins (1993) on the four-kingdom schema not read directly.
